transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. What brings you here today?

Yeah, um… I guess I came in because things have just been kind of off since my father-in-law moved in with us. I’m still keeping it together at work — I’m an EMT, so you kind of have to, you know, there’s not a lot of room to be scattered on calls — but when I get home, I’m more wound up. Shorter with people than I’d like.

And I’m taking some coursework too, and that’s been harder to stay on top of. I used to clear my head with fishing, woodworking, those first-aid workshops I help with sometimes… well, attend or help, depending on the week. I haven’t really been going. It sounds small, but those were kind of my release valves, I guess. Since the move-in, I just feel like I’m not handling things the way I normally do.
Have you noticed that you’re not enjoying the things you used to, like fishing or woodworking, as much as you did before?

Yeah… I mean, I still like the idea of them, if that makes sense. Fishing, woodworking — those used to kind of reset me. Same with the first-aid workshops, even after doing EMT work all week, which sounds funny, but it’s a different gear, you know?

Lately, since my father-in-law moved in, I just… I don’t go. I tell myself I’ll get to it after coursework or after things settle at home, and then I’m too wound up or short with people and I skip it. Work I can still hold together, because you have to, but those things that normally clear my head have kind of fallen off.
Have you noticed that you’ve lost interest in doing things like fishing, woodworking, or attending first-aid workshops, even when you have the time?

Yeah, I think so… I mean, it’s not that I suddenly hate fishing or woodworking or anything. If I picture being out there with a line in the water, or just sanding something in the garage, I still think, yeah, that would probably help.

But ever since my father-in-law moved in with us, things at home just feel… tighter, I guess. I’m holding it together at work, because on calls you don’t really get to be distracted, but then I get home and I’m wound up. And with coursework too, I get behind or irritated, and then those things — fishing, the woodworking, the first-aid workshops — I just skip them. Even when I technically have the time, I don’t seem to get myself there.
Has there been a time recently when you didn’t feel like doing things you used to enjoy, like fishing or woodworking, even if you had the chance?

Yeah… there have been a few times. Like, I’ll have a window where I could go fishing or mess around with a woodworking project, and instead I just kind of… don’t. I tell myself I should, because those things usually clear my head.

It really started after my father-in-law moved in with us. I’m still doing okay at work — with EMT stuff, you sort of have to stay on point — but once I’m home, I’m more wound up, shorter than I want to be. And then with coursework on top of it, I get stuck in that “I’ll do it later” mode.

So yeah, even when I technically have the chance, I’ve been skipping the fishing, woodworking, and even those first-aid workshops that used to help me feel a little more like myself.
Has there been a time in the past two weeks when you felt no interest or pleasure in activities you used to enjoy, even when things at home were calmer or you had the time to do them?

Yeah… I think in the last couple weeks, yes. Not like I never care about those things anymore, but I’ve had time where I could’ve gone fishing or gone out to the garage and done some woodworking, and I just didn’t.

It’s really been since my father-in-law moved in with us. I’m still holding it together at work — you kind of have to in EMT work, there’s no room to be half-there — but then I get home and I’m wound up. And then I’ll think, “Well, maybe I should go to one of those first-aid workshops,” which is funny because it’s still medical stuff, but it usually clears my head in a different way. And instead I just skip it.

Even when the house is a little calmer, I’m still sort of carrying it, if that makes sense. I end up being shorter than I mean to be, or thinking about coursework I’m behind on, and the stuff that usually helps me reset just doesn’t happen.
Over the past two weeks, have you felt a lack of interest or pleasure in activities you used to enjoy, like fishing or woodworking, for most of the day, nearly every day?

Not most of the day, nearly every day, no… I don’t think I’d say it that strongly. It’s more like since my father-in-law moved in, I’ve been holding it together at work, and then when I get home I’m wound up and short, and the coursework starts hanging over me.

So the fishing, woodworking, those first-aid workshops — they’re still things I know usually help clear my head, but I’ve been skipping them more. Like I’ll have the chance and then just… not go. But it’s not like all day every day I feel no pleasure in anything. It feels more tied to the stress at home.
Have you been feeling down or sad, even when things at home are relatively calm or the stress with your father-in-law isn’t front of mind?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way. I mean, I get worn down, sure, and sometimes I’m quieter than usual, but “down or sad” when things are actually calm… I don’t know.

Sometimes it’s hard to separate, because even when nobody’s actively arguing or needing something, I’m still kind of thinking about the whole situation. Like at home, calm doesn’t always feel calm, if that makes sense. It reminds me of being on shift, actually — even when the radio’s quiet, you’re still listening for it. But that’s probably not what you’re asking.

So… I guess I haven’t really noticed myself feeling sad out of nowhere. It’s more that I feel weighed on when the home stuff is in the background.
Have you noticed that you’ve stopped enjoying things in general, even activities outside of work or home stress, like hobbies or time with friends?

I wouldn’t say I’ve stopped enjoying things in general, exactly. It’s more like… ever since my father-in-law moved in with us, I’m using up a lot of energy just keeping it together at work, and then when I’m home I’m wound up and shorter than I want to be.

And then my coursework is sitting there too, which doesn’t help. So the things that normally clear my head — fishing, woodworking, even those first-aid workshops I like going to — I’ve started skipping them. Not because I hate them now or anything, just… I don’t seem to get myself there. It’s more tied up with all this home stress than feeling like nothing is enjoyable anymore.
Have you ever felt like you’ve completely lost interest in almost everything, even things you really used to enjoy, for most of the day — not just occasionally, but nearly every day?

I don’t think so… not completely, no. I mean, I know I’ve been saying I’ve skipped stuff more, and that’s true, but “almost everything, most of the day, nearly every day” feels bigger than what’s been happening.

It’s more like I get home and I’m already sort of braced, you know? Like when you’re on a call and you’re waiting for the next thing to go sideways — sorry, that’s probably not the best comparison. But I don’t feel like I’ve lost interest in everything. I just don’t always follow through on the things that usually help me unwind.
Over the past two weeks, have you felt a loss of interest or pleasure in nearly all activities, including things you usually enjoy, most of the day, nearly every day?

I’m still not sure I’d call it that. Nearly all activities, most of the day, nearly every day… that sounds pretty constant, and I don’t think that’s what I’m noticing.

I mean, there are things I don’t get around to lately, but that’s different than having no interest or no pleasure in anything. Some days I’ll think, “I should go do something,” and then I just… don’t. But I don’t know if that answers what you’re asking. I haven’t really been tracking it like that.
Over the past two weeks, have you felt a loss of interest or pleasure in activities you usually enjoy, like fishing or woodworking, on most days?

Most days… yeah, I guess I have been skipping them more than I used to. Fishing, woodworking, those first-aid workshops — those are usually the things that sort of reset me.

But I don’t know if it’s that I don’t enjoy them anymore. It’s more like since my father-in-law moved in, I’m holding it together all day at work, and then I get home and there’s coursework sitting there, and I’m already wound up. So instead of going out to the garage or making plans, I just don’t. It’s like I run out of room in my head.

Over the past two weeks, have you found that you’re not getting the same sense of enjoyment or pleasure from activities like fishing, woodworking, or attending first-aid workshops, even when you do manage to do them?

I’m not sure I can say that clearly. I haven’t really noticed it like, “Oh, I’m doing the thing but it feels flat.” It’s more that I don’t get to the point of doing it as much.

Like with woodworking, if I’m actually out there and I get focused on measuring something or sanding a piece down right, I can still kind of get into it. Though then I’ll remember I left something inside or I should be checking on something, and—sorry, that’s not really what you asked.

So… I don’t know. I haven’t paid attention to whether the enjoyment itself is different. I just know I’m not doing those things as often.
Over the past two weeks, have you felt a loss of interest or pleasure in most activities — including things you usually enjoy — for most of the day, nearly every day?

I don’t know that I can honestly answer it that cleanly. “Most activities, most of the day, nearly every day” sounds like something I’d notice as a definite pattern, and I’m not sure I have.

I mean, I’ve been off, sure, but then I think about work and how some days you come home and you’re just… done. Back when I started as an EMT, I used to be better about carving out time for myself, but now I’ll get home and everything feels like it’s stacked up. So I might not start anything I enjoy.

But loss of pleasure in most things all day? I don’t know. I wouldn’t want to say yes if I’m not sure that’s really what’s happening.
Over the past two weeks, have you felt a loss of interest or pleasure in activities you usually enjoy, like fishing or woodworking, on most days?

Yeah, I mean… on most days I’ve been skipping those things, more than actually feeling like I hate them or they don’t matter anymore.

Fishing and woodworking usually clear my head, and even the first-aid workshops help me feel like I’m keeping sharp. But since my father-in-law moved in with us, I’m holding it together at work all day, and then I get home and there’s coursework and everything feels kind of piled up. So I get wound up and short, and instead of going out to the garage or making time for fishing, I just don’t.

patient.answer:
I’m still not sure I’d call it that. Nearly all activities, most of the day, nearly every day… that sounds pretty constant, and I don’t think that’s what I’m noticing.

I mean, there are things I don’t get around to lately, but that’s different than having no interest or no pleasure in anything. Some days I’ll think, “I should go do something,” and then I just… don’t. But I don’t know if that answers what you’re asking. I haven’t really been tracking it like that.

inference.note: The patient continues to describe stress-related difficulties tied to situational factors (father-in-law moving in) without meeting criteria for major depressive disorder or persistent loss of interest/pleasure across all domains. Adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood (F43.22) remains relevant, as well as acute stress reaction (F43.0) and unspecified stress-related disorder (F43.8). No further narrowing possible at this time.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a significant reduction in interest or pleasure in activities, specifically fishing or woodworking, most days for at least two weeks, which would support a diagnosis of a major depressive episode.
doctor.question: Over the past two weeks, have you felt a loss of interest or pleasure in activities you usually enjoy, like fishing or woodworking, on most days?

target_item.name: Stress_Related_Maladaptive_Response
target_item.manifestation: I came in because ever since my father-in-law moved in with us, I’ve been holding it together at work, but at home and with my coursework I’m more wound up and short than I’m used to, and I’ve started skipping the fishing, woodworking, and first-aid workshops that usually keep my head clear.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about reduced interest or pleasure in usual enjoyable activities like fishing or woodworking, which is covered by the stress-related response where I’ve been skipping those activities since the caregiving stress began.

patient.answer:
Most days… yeah, I guess I have been skipping them more than I used to. Fishing, woodworking, those first-aid workshops — those are usually the things that sort of reset me.

But I don’t know if it’s that I don’t enjoy them anymore. It’s more like since my father-in-law moved in, I’m holding it together all day at work, and then I get home and there’s coursework sitting there, and I’m already wound up. So instead of going out to the garage or making plans, I just don’t. It’s like I run out of room in my head.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a diminished ability to experience pleasure (anhedonia) in specific previously enjoyed activities, on most days over the past two weeks, which is a key criterion for major depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Over the past two weeks, have you found that you’re not getting the same sense of enjoyment or pleasure from activities like fishing, woodworking, or attending first-aid workshops, even when you do manage to do them?

target_item.reason: The question asks specifically about reduced enjoyment or pleasure during activities when they are actually done, but the symptom profile only describes skipping those activities due to stress and feeling wound up, not loss of pleasure while doing them.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I can say that clearly. I haven’t really noticed it like, “Oh, I’m doing the thing but it feels flat.” It’s more that I don’t get to the point of doing it as much.

Like with woodworking, if I’m actually out there and I get focused on measuring something or sanding a piece down right, I can still kind of get into it. Though then I’ll remember I left something inside or I should be checking on something, and—sorry, that’s not really what you asked.

So… I don’t know. I haven’t paid attention to whether the enjoyment itself is different. I just know I’m not doing those things as often.

inference.note: This turn did not rule out or confirm any specific disorder definitively. The patient's responses continue to suggest stress-related symptoms without clear evidence of a major depressive episode or persistent loss of interest/pleasure in activities. Adjustment Disorder (F43.22), Acute Stress Reaction (F43.0), and Other Reactions to Severe Stress (F43.8) remain plausible. Further clarification is needed to determine if symptoms meet criteria for a diagnosable condition or are better accounted for by situational stress.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a significant reduction in interest or pleasure in most activities, including those previously enjoyed, for most of the day, nearly every day over the past two weeks — a key criterion for major depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Over the past two weeks, have you felt a loss of interest or pleasure in most activities — including things you usually enjoy — for most of the day, nearly every day?

target_item.reason: The question is asking specifically about loss of interest or pleasure in most activities nearly every day over the past two weeks, which is not directly covered by the adjustment-disorder symptom profile; the profile describes stress-related skipping of activities rather than clear pervasive anhedonia.

patient.answer:
I don’t know that I can honestly answer it that cleanly. “Most activities, most of the day, nearly every day” sounds like something I’d notice as a definite pattern, and I’m not sure I have.

I mean, I’ve been off, sure, but then I think about work and how some days you come home and you’re just… done. Back when I started as an EMT, I used to be better about carving out time for myself, but now I’ll get home and everything feels like it’s stacked up. So I might not start anything I enjoy.

But loss of pleasure in most things all day? I don’t know. I wouldn’t want to say yes if I’m not sure that’s really what’s happening.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a persistent loss of interest or pleasure in activities they usually enjoy, specifically most days over the past two weeks.
doctor.question: Over the past two weeks, have you felt a loss of interest or pleasure in activities you usually enjoy, like fishing or woodworking, on most days?

target_item.name: Stress_Related_Maladaptive_Response
target_item.manifestation: I came in because ever since my father-in-law moved in with us, I’ve been holding it together at work, but at home and with my coursework I’m more wound up and short than I’m used to, and I’ve started skipping the fishing, woodworking, and first-aid workshops that usually keep my head clear.
target_item.reason: The question asks about reduced interest or pleasure in usual activities like fishing and woodworking, which is reflected in the stress-related response of skipping these activities since the father-in-law moved in.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I mean… on most days I’ve been skipping those things, more than actually feeling like I hate them or they don’t matter anymore.

Fishing and woodworking usually clear my head, and even the first-aid workshops help me feel like I’m keeping sharp. But since my father-in-law moved in with us, I’m holding it together at work all day, and then I get home and there’s coursework and everything feels kind of piled up. So I get wound up and short, and instead of going out to the garage or making time for fishing, I just don’t.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms are primarily related to stress from the recent family situation (father-in-law moving in) affecting their ability to engage in previously enjoyed activities, but without pervasive loss of pleasure or interest across all domains. This aligns more clearly with F43.22 (Adjustment Disorder with Mixed Anxiety and Depressed Mood) and rules out F43.0 (Acute Stress Reaction) due to the prolonged and situational nature of the symptoms. F43.8 (Other Reactions to Severe Stress, Not Elsewhere Classified) is also ruled out as the symptoms fit within the criteria for F43.22.
